sentences.text: Listracanthus is known primarily from its tremendous, feather-like denticles that can reach up to four inches in length.
These structures featured a large main spine with secondary spines radiating from the sides like feather barbs or a comb.
The main denticles were located on the vertebral column, with secondary spines emanating from the skin like a feather or a comb.
Its denticles are so large they can measure up to four inches.
Based on Zangerl's account, Ray Troll reconstructed the animal as resembling a shark with feathers.
The genus Listracanthus was described by Newberry and Worthen in 1870.
The type species of the genus Listracanthus is Listracanthus hystrix.
Listracanthus is classified within the family Edestidae, and known species include L. beyrichi, L. eliasi, L. hildrethi, L. hystrix, L. pectenatus, L. wardi, and L. woltersi.
Listracanthus lived from the Late Carboniferous to the Early Triassic, first appearing in Late Carboniferous strata in North America.
It disappeared during the Upper Triassic, making it one of the longest-lived genera in the family Edestidae.
There are 22 recorded fossil occurrences of the genus Listracanthus in the Paleobiology Database.

Some authors suggest Listracanthus may be a member of Menaspiformes because denticles similar to those of Listracanthus have been found with remains of that group, despite the lack of eel-like bodies in those fossils.
